summary: This informational memo discusses how useful various tests for measuring single-router OSPF convergence are. One part covers the advantages and limits of specific benchmarks, and the other covers how to interpret the results.

eli5.summary: A speed test is only helpful if you know what it can and cannot tell you. This document explains the strengths and weaknesses of tests for OSPF routers.

questions: how to interpret ospf benchmark results
why are ospf benchmarks hard to compare across vendors
subtitle: When OSPF convergence benchmarks work well and when they mislead.

tldr.problem: OSPF convergence benchmarks are useful but have limits and assumptions. Operators and engineers sometimes misapply them, leading to wrong conclusions about router performance.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC explains the strengths and weaknesses of OSPF benchmarking tests, documents practical pitfalls observed when implementing tests, and discusses how topology and LSA choices affect results.
tldr.outcome: Engineers can now run OSPF benchmarks more effectively and interpret results more accurately.

facts.label: Key assumptions
facts.value: Immediate duplicate LSA ACK, non-preemptive SPF, single-threaded design

facts.label: SPF algorithm complexity
facts.value: Linear (O(n)) for tree, quadratic (O(n²)) for mesh

facts.label: Factors affecting results
facts.value: LSA mix, topology shape, tree structure, meshiness

today: RFC 4063 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. It remains the standard reference for understanding the applicability and limitations of OSPF convergence benchmarks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Benchmarking OSPF convergence is useful, but the tests have limitations. Understanding both the advantages and pitfalls is essential before running tests or interpreting results. This RFC discusses why these tests matter, what assumptions they make, and when they can mislead.

The document includes two main parts: first, the advantages and assumptions of the tests, including their limitations; second, practical observations from implementing the tests and factors that significantly affect results, such as the shape of the network topology and how LSAs are ordered during testing.
sections.eli5: Before you trust the results of a speed test, understand what it actually measures, what it assumes, and what it does not tell you.

sections.title: Why Benchmark OSPF
sections.content:
OSPF benchmarks are valuable for several purposes. Comparing versions: Different versions of the same router's OSPF implementation can be tested to find where improvements have been made. Performance prediction: A network operator planning to deploy a router in a specific location can run benchmarks that emulate the exact conditions (topology and LSA load) that will exist at that site, yielding real-world performance estimates.

Measuring across scenarios: Benchmarks reveal how OSPF performance varies with network size, link types, and LSA counts. Research: Researchers studying routing can use benchmark measurements as input parameters for OSPF simulations. Optimization: Understanding the delay required for individual tasks (like SPF computation or route installation) helps operators tune timers and resource allocation to avoid network overload.
sections.eli5: Benchmarks help you pick the right router for your network, see if you are getting better, and help researchers understand how routing works.

sections.title: Limitations and Assumptions
sections.content:
The RFC 4061 tests make several assumptions that may not hold in all implementations. Tests assume duplicate LSAs are acknowledged immediately, but some implementations delay ACKs, which breaks the test logic. Tests assume SPF is non-preemptive (once it starts, it runs to completion), but if SPF can be interrupted by other tasks, measurements include idle time and are inflated.

Multithreaded implementations may behave differently than single-threaded ones. Convergence time does not include forwarding plane installation, so the time a router reports as converged may not match the time packets start using the new path. Tests also focus on individual components and may not accurately predict large-scale network behavior. Finally, comparisons across vendors require caution: different implementations have different architectures, resources, and design trade-offs, so faster convergence in one test does not necessarily mean the product is faster in production.
sections.eli5: The tests assume all routers are built the same way, but they are not. Also, the test measures one thing, not the real world.

sections.title: Practical Challenges
sections.content:
Measuring SPF time externally is the hardest test to perform accurately. The timing of the duplicate LSA is critical: send it too soon and the router has not started SPF yet; send it too late and SPF is already done. Multiple test runs with different delays are often needed to find the right timing. Some implementations add delays between successive SPF runs (SPF hold time or SPF delay), which inflates measurements—these intervals should be subtracted from results.

The measurement device itself introduces noise: packet processing delays and output delays blur the exact moment an event occurs. To reduce noise, increase the number of samples, timestamp packets as early as possible (ideally in the kernel), keep the measurement device lightly loaded, and establish a baseline understanding of measurement noise. Understanding the OSPF implementation being tested—how it batches LSAs, when it installs routes, whether multithreading is used—significantly improves measurement accuracy.
sections.eli5: Measuring SPF is tricky because timing is everything. Also, the measurement tool is not perfect; it adds its own delays.

sections.title: What Affects Benchmark Results
sections.content:
The mix of LSAs injected during testing significantly affects results. The number of destinations matters: more destinations mean longer route installation times. LSA types matter: type 1 (router), type 2 (network), and external LSAs have different processing costs. LSA quantity affects SPF algorithm complexity. LSA order can skew results if it happens to favor the router's internal data structures; LSAs should be randomly ordered.

Network topology shape is critical. The SPF algorithm's runtime depends on the tree structure: a linear tree (1-1-1 chain) runs in O(n) time, but a balanced binary tree runs in O(n²). A fully meshed network is also O(n²). Real networks are typically sparser; emulated topologies should match the mix of tree depth, meshiness, and branch factor of real networks to yield realistic measurements. Operators should use routes taken from the actual deployment site when possible.
sections.eli5: Test results depend on what roads you draw, how many roads, and in what order you add them to the test.
